title: Twenty-Three Armies Against Mathura
story:
Asti and Prapti, the daughters of Jarasandha, king of Magadha, came to their father's court the way grief comes: slowly, and with everything already known. They had been given in marriage to Kamsa of Mathura; now they stood before him as widows and told him of it. Jarasandha heard the unwelcome news, and grief and anger rose in him together.

He had owed Kamsa a debt. The dead man had been his son-in-law and his ally, a king who had chained up his own father and ruled Mathura with Jarasandha's backing, holding the Yadava clans in check while Jarasandha filled his prisons with the kings of the world. Now the Yadavas had killed him. Krishna and Balarama had struck Kamsa down, and Ugrasena, the father Kamsa had imprisoned, had become king in his place, with the Bhojas, the Vrishnis and the Andhakas, the clans of the Yadavas, gathered around him. The debt was unpaid, and Jarasandha resolved to make the earth free of Yadavas, to wipe the whole race away in a single campaign. Burning like fire, making every possible arrangement, in no time at all the king of Magadha was marching on Mathura.

And the kings he had conquered marched with him. Some came for fear of Jarasandha, some out of jealousy of Krishna, some because he had beaten them and they had nowhere else to stand. His friends, his relatives and his allies came too, each at the head of his own army. Dantavakra of Karusha came, and the powerful king of Chedi; the king of Kalinga; Bhishmaka with his son Rukmi; the kings of Anga and Vanga, of Koshala and Kashi and Dasharna; Bhagadatta, the lord of the Yavanas; Suvala of Gandhara; Duryodhana and the other sons of Dhritarashtra. King after king, chariot-warriors every one, they followed him, each camping in his own place.

They entered the province of Shurasena, a land of barley fields and woodlands, and the order went out: lay siege on every side to this city. Twenty-three akshauhinis ringed Mathura, and an akshauhini was an army of its own, thousands upon thousands of chariots, elephants and horses. So great was the host that the horizon turned to dust and metal, and the ground beneath the city's walls trembled under the weight of it.

From the walls, Krishna watched the host settle around Mathura like a sea risen over its banks. He had come into the world in a human body on purpose, to work in it as a man works, and a man who means to solve a problem does not wave it away. He did not wish the army gone, or turn the siege aside with a gesture. He looked at it long and carefully, the way a man looks at a thing he means to solve, weighing the twenty-three armies, and the kings behind them, and the city, and the people inside it.

Around the walls, the fires of the besieging host burned through the night, ringing Mathura like a second horizon. The siege had begun, and the first night of it belonged to the besiegers. Inside the city, Krishna was still thinking, for a king who looks on such an army must first decide what he is willing to do.
reflection: Krishna meets the greatest army ever raised against him not with a miracle but with deliberation. The old phrase kāraṇa-mānuṣaḥ — one whose humanity is his instrument — is the point: he refuses to solve the siege by sheer divinity, choosing instead to think, plan, and act as a man among men.
tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana compresses this whole conflict into one line — Jarasandha attacked eighteen times and was routed each time — while the Harivamsha narrates the march and the siege separately and gives the invading force six divisions. This story follows the Bhagavata Purana's number of twenty-three akshauhinis.
next_story_tease: And as Krishna thought, a divine chariot with celestial weapons was descending from the sky toward Mathura.
hero_scene: Krishna on the walls of Mathura gazing out at Jarasandha's encircling army of twenty-three akshauhinis, spread across the plain like a risen sea, its campfires already burning against the dusk.
